section.title: Chapter review and projects
section.p: This chapter began with a simple move: instead of forcing a curve to be a graph y=f(x), let a moving point draw it.
That one move opened many doors.
A circle could be traced by
A rolling wheel produced a cycloid.
A rotating ray produced polar coordinates.
A focus and directrix produced conics.
A point x+iy became a complex number, and multiplication became scaling plus rotation.

subsection.title: Chapter map

row.cell: Graphs that pass the vertical line test; ordinary derivative and integral formulas.
Curves traced by motion, loops, cusps, rolling curves, and curves not expressible as one graph.
Rotation, spirals, radial distance, roses, limacons, and conics with a focus at the pole.
Scaling, rotation, circular motion, oscillation, and the preview of Euler’s formula.

subsection.p: No coordinate system is universally best. The skill is knowing which one makes the structure visible.

exercise.title: Why is a parametrization more than a Cartesian equation?

statement.p: A Cartesian equation describes a set of points. In your own words, what extra questions can a parametrization or polar tracing answer, and why do length and area formulas need those answers?

hint.p: Orientation, speed, starting point, and repeated tracing affect integrals of speed and signed area. The formula follows the motion it is given.

exercise.title: When is polar form the right language for a conic?

statement.p: An ellipse centered at the origin and an ellipse with a focus at the pole tell different stories. In your own words, why does planetary motion prefer the polar description, and what extra law besides the shape of the orbit is needed?

hint.p: The sun sits at a focus, so distance from the pole is the physically important coordinate. Kepler’s second law is about motion along that shape, not about the shape alone.

subsection.title: The bridge to infinite series
subsection.p: The chapter ends with a preview that has not yet been proved:
This formula says that an exponential can move around a circle.
But why should an exponential know anything about sine and cosine?
The proof comes from a new kind of infinite process. Not an infinite subdivision of an area. Not an infinite limiting process of slopes. This time the infinite process is an infinite sum:
subsection.md: \text{Calculus now turns from curves and coordinates to sequences and infinite series.}

exercise.title: What new idea does treating the plane as a number system add?

statement.p: Complex multiplication scales and rotates. In your own words, how does that continue the chapter’s move from graphs to motions, and why does Euler’s formula point toward infinite series rather than finish the story here?

hint.p: The same plane can be a pair of coordinates, a polar pair, or one complex number. Proving e^{i\theta}=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta requires an infinite sum of functions.
